title: The Year of the Elephant
subtitle: Before his birth, the world already bowed to his coming
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the opening of the biography
Qur'an 105 (Surah Al-Fil) — the armies of the elephant

chapters.heading: Abraha's Army and the Falling Birds
chapters.body: In the year the Prophet ﷺ was born, Abraha al-Ashram, the Christian ruler of Yemen, built a magnificent cathedral in Sana'a — and then marched on Makkah with elephants to pull the Arabs away from the Kaaba to his new shrine. The Qur'an compressed that arrogance into five verses: 'Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant? Did He not make their plot go astray, and send against them birds in flocks, striking them with stones of hard clay, and He made them like eaten straw?' (105:1-5). The seerah of Ibn Ishaq records what the Arabs called that year forever after: the Year of the Elephant — the year the Kabah humbled an empire, in the year the boy was born (the date is a seerah report) who would make that humble House the qiblah of the world. From his first breath, history arranged itself around him.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: Allah defended His House with birds. What big threat in your life might look smaller if you remembered Who is defending you?

title: The Orphan of Makkah
subtitle: Amina's son, Halimah's milk, Abu Talib's shadow
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the fosterage and the opening years
Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — Halimah's account of the fosterage (not from the six books; Not yet scholar-reviewed)

chapters.heading: The Child Who Brought Blessing
chapters.body: Muhammad ﷺ was born in the Year of the Elephant, son of Abdullah ibn Abdul-Muttalib and Amina bint Wahb. His father died before his birth, and by desert custom he was given to a foster mother of Banu Sa'd — and the seerah records that Halimah's household, poor and dry, blossomed the moment she took him: her flock fattened, her milk flowed, and she pressed to keep the child an extra season (seerah report: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham; not from the six books). At six, his mother Amina died on the road home from Madinah at a place called Abwa, and the boy came back to Makkah an orphan twice over. His grandfather Abdul-Muttalib took him in and adored him — keeping the child beside him in the council of Quraysh where no child had ever sat — and when the old man died, Muhammad ﷺ passed to his uncle Abu Talib, who guarded him for forty years. The Qur'an would one day name his condition over him: 'Did He not find you an orphan and shelter you?' (93:6). Orphanhood was his first teacher; protection was his Lord's first gift.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: The Prophet ﷺ lost his parents as a small child and was still raised with love. Who shelters the vulnerable people around you — and could that be you?

title: Al-Amin, The Trustworthy
subtitle: The honest young man the Quraysh could not bribe
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1 pp. 187-189 and 198 (Maysarah, the marriage, al-Amin), read on shamela.ws, book 23833
Sahih al-Bukhari 3 — Khadijah's testimony to his character

chapters.heading: The Merchant of Makkah
chapters.body: As a young man Muhammad ﷺ was known among Quraysh for the truth of his speech and his great trustworthiness, and Khadijah bint Khuwaylid, a woman of standing who hired men to trade with her wealth, sent him to Syria with her slave Maysarah on better terms than she gave other merchants (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 p. 188). The goods sold for double or close to it. Maysarah told her what he had seen, including, in his report, two angels shading Muhammad ﷺ from the sun; that is Maysarah's report as Ibn Ishaq passes it on, not a hadith. Khadijah then sent to him and said that she wished to marry him because of his kinship, his standing among his people, his trustworthiness, his good character and the truth of his speech (p. 189); a footnote names Nafisa bint Munya as the go-between on another account. She is given as forty and he twenty-five (p. 187; a note says another view makes her forty-five). Years later, when revelation first shook him, her answer named the character of his whole youth: 'You keep good relations with your kin, you help the weak, you honor the guest, you bear the hardship of the road, you help against the calamities of truth' (Sahih al-Bukhari 3). And Ibn Hisham notes that before revelation Quraysh called him al-Amin, the Trustworthy (p. 198).
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Khadijah listed five habits that proved his prophethood. Which of the five — kin, the weak, guests, hardship, truth — needs your work this month?

title: The Cave of Hira
subtitle: Forty years of silence before the first word
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the retreat to Hira
Sahih al-Bukhari 3 — Aisha's narration of the first revelation
Qur'an 96:1-5 — the first revealed words

chapters.heading: Solitude Before the Storm
chapters.body: In his late thirties, Muhammad ﷺ began leaving Makkah's noise for the cave of Hira on Jabal an-Nur, taking provisions and turning his face to the silence. The seerah records that he would stay days at a time in the cave, thinking — a man of Makkah withdrawing from Makkah, troubled by the idols he had never bowed to. In the month of Ramadan, in the year he turned forty, the silence ended. The angel came to him and said: Iqra — Read. He answered: I am not one who can read. The angel embraced him until it was more than he could bear, then released him and repeated the command — three times — until the words descended: 'Read in the name of your Lord who created, created man from a clot. Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen, taught man what he did not know' (96:1-5). The first word of the final revelation was not a command to rule or to fight. It was a command to read, in the name of the One who created — and the first description of the Lord it gave was not power, but generosity (96:3).

chapters.heading: Khadijah's Test
chapters.body: He ran home from the cave trembling, asking to be covered, and told Khadijah what he had seen — and her response, preserved in Bukhari's Sahih, became the first theology of the new religion: 'Never! By Allah, Allah will never disgrace you. You keep good relations with your kin, you help the weak, you honor the guest, you bear the hardship of the road, you help against the calamities of truth' (Bukhari 3). Notice: his wife reasoned from character to truth. Then she took him to her cousin Waraqa ibn Nawfal, a Christian scholar, who heard the description and said the words that confirmed everything: 'This is the same one who keeps the secrets whom Allah had sent to Moses' (Bukhari 3). The first consultant of the prophethood was a woman; the first confirmation came from a Christian scholar who knew the scriptures. From its first hour, this message crossed every boundary people build.

familyQuestion: The first command of the final revelation was Iqra — Read. What is your relationship with reading — and could one good book change your family's next year?

title: Three Years of Whispers
subtitle: The secret call — the first believers
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the private preaching
Qur'an 26:214 — 'warn your nearest kindred'
Musnad Ahmad — Ali's account of the meal for Banu Hashim (number not verified; Disputed in the sources)

chapters.heading: The Call and the Feast
chapters.body: For three years the call moved quietly — from house to house, trusted friend to trusted friend. The seerah reports name Khadijah, Ali, Zayd and Abu Bakr among the first to believe (the order is discussed in the sources) — a woman, a youth, a freed slave, a merchant: the future of the ummah in miniature. When the command came — 'And warn your nearest kindred' (26:214) — Muhammad ﷺ climbed Safa and called the clans of Quraysh, asking them: if I told you horsemen were in this valley, would you believe me? They said: yes, we have never found you but truthful. He said: then I am a warner before a severe punishment (reported in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). Abu Lahab cursed him and left — and a verse descended on that day naming the uncle's end (111:1-5). Disputed in the sources — the account of a meal for Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib is reported in Musnad Ahmad (the number was not verified) and its wording is contested: 'Which of you will assist me in this matter, so that he is my brother, my executor, my successor among you?' The room fell silent — and Ali, barely into his teens, stood and said: I will, though I am the youngest. Muhammad ﷺ placed his hand on Ali's neck and said: this is my brother, my successor among you.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: The first believers were a woman, a teenager, and a freed slave. What does that tell you about whose hearts Allah chooses first?

title: Bilal and the Heavy Sand
subtitle: The slave who taught the world a word: Ahad
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1 pp. 317-318 (the torture of the oppressed; Bilal; Abu Bakr frees six), read on shamela.ws, book 23833

chapters.heading: Ahad, Ahad
chapters.body: When the call went public and Quraysh could not bribe or debate it down, they turned on believers who had no clan to shield them. Ibn Ishaq says they tortured the oppressed with beating, hunger, thirst and the heat of Makkah's sand (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 p. 317). Bilal's master was Umayyah ibn Khalaf; at midday Bilal was laid on his back in the valley of Makkah with a great rock on his chest and told he would stay so until he died or denied Muhammad ﷺ, and he kept saying: Ahad, Ahad — One, One (p. 318). Abu Bakr told Umayyah to fear Allah, and offered him a stronger black slave of his own in exchange; Umayyah accepted and Abu Bakr freed Bilal. Ibn Hisham lists six whom Abu Bakr freed at that time, among them Amir ibn Fuhayra, Umm Ubays and Zunayra (p. 318). Bilal, Ammar, Sumayyah, Suhayb, Khabbab: the weak of Makkah are remembered because the truth did not need the strong to survive. It needed the sincere.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Bilal had one word under a boulder: Ahad. If your faith cost you comfort today, what would your one word be?

title: The Night of the Journey
subtitle: Al-Isra wal-Mi'raj — five prayers as the gift of the heavens
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 349 — the full narration of the Night Journey
Qur'an 17:1 — 'Exalted is He who took His servant by night'
Sahih Muslim 162 — the fifty prayers reduced to five

chapters.heading: From the Haram to the Farthest Mosque
chapters.body: The Prophet ﷺ was carried from the sacred mosque to the farthest mosque in a single night: 'Exalted is He who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, whose surroundings We have blessed' (17:1). From Jerusalem he ascended through the heavens — Bukhari preserves the narration in full — past Adam at the first heaven, Isa and Yahya, Yusuf, Idris, Harun, Musa, and Ibrahim leaning against the Bayt al-Ma'mur, to the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary. Musa asked him at the end what his nation had been given, and when he heard fifty prayers a day, Musa said: your people cannot bear fifty — go back and ask your Lord to lighten it (Bukhari 349, Muslim 162). He returned and returned again, until the covenant stood at five prayers for the reward of fifty — until, in the narration, the word came: they are five, and they are fifty; My word is not changed (Muslim 162). The five daily prayers are not a burden negotiated down. They are a gift negotiated up — from the Lord of the heavens, through the stubborn love of Musa for the believers, to your doorstep five times a day.

familyQuestion: Five prayers were gifted from above the seven heavens. Do you treat them as a burden negotiated down — or a gift you get to keep?

title: The Boycott
subtitle: Three years in the valley — the written siege
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the document of the boycott
Qur'an 111 — 'May the hands of Abu Lahab perish'

chapters.heading: A Document Against a Clan
chapters.body: When persuasion, bribery, and torture failed, Quraysh tried isolation. The clans wrote a document — the seerah records its hanging inside the Kaaba — binding themselves: no marrying the Banu Hashim, no selling to them, no sitting with them, until they surrendered Muhammad ﷺ to be killed. The document turned Makkah into a prison for one clan. For three years the Hashim and al-Muttalib, Muslims and non-Muslims among them alike, ate leaves and the milk of a single she-camel, in the stony valley outside the city. Khadijah's wealth drained away in those years — the seerah historians count the boycott among the causes of her death soon after. And then the tide turned from an unexpected place: some Qurayshis themselves, sickened by watching relatives starve, began passing food secretly; then Hisham ibn Amr and others worked openly until the document — which, the tradition records, termites had devoured except the words 'in Your name, O Allah' — was declared void by the very men who wrote it. A starving clan had outlasted an empire's merchant aristocracy, and the famine broke before the faith did.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: The boycott starved the Muslims for three years but broke before their faith did. What pressure are you under that only feels permanent?

title: The First Hijrah
subtitle: Abyssinia — the king whose bishops wept and refused the extradition
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the emigration to Abyssinia
Musnad Ahmad — Ja'far's speech before the Negus (number not verified)

chapters.heading: A Kingdom That Let Them Pray
chapters.body: When the persecution of the weak believers became unbearable, the Prophet ﷺ told the believers: go to Abyssinia — there is a king there under whom no one is wronged. It was the first emigration of the Muslim community: no army, no land promised, just a king they had never met. And when the Quraysh sent envoys with gifts to demand their extradition, the Negus convened his bishops — and the bishops, like professionals everywhere, asked about doctrine before character. Ja'far ibn Abi Talib answered by reciting from Surah Maryam — and the king and his priests wept until their beards were wet, and the Negus refused the extradition with the sentence history remembers: go, for by Allah, I will never surrender you to them (reported by Ahmad; the number was not verified). A Christian kingdom had become the first refuge of Islam — proof that truth recognizes truth across every border.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: The Negus protected strangers he had no reason to protect. Have you ever been protected by a stranger — or been one for someone else?

title: The Conversion of Umar
subtitle: The man who set out to kill the Prophet ﷺ became his shield
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1 pp. 343-345 (the conversion narrative up to the knock at the door), read on shamela.ws, book 23833
Sahih al-Bukhari 3680 — the Prophet's ﷺ dream of Umar's palace in Paradise

chapters.heading: A Lion Changes Direction
chapters.body: Umar ibn al-Khattab set out, girded with his sword, to kill the Prophet ﷺ (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 p. 343). On the way Nu'aym ibn Abdullah, who was secretly Muslim, sent him to his own house first: Khabbab used to visit his sister Fatima bint al-Khattab to teach her the Qur'an, and her husband Sa'id ibn Zayd was also a Muslim (pp. 343-344). Umar struck his sister and wounded her; a page headed 'Ta-Ha' was in the house (p. 344). Then, in this account, he washed because she said only the pure may touch it, took the page and read it, and said: how fine this speech is, and how noble (p. 345). Khabbab came out and told him of the Prophet's ﷺ prayer that Islam be strengthened by Abu al-Hakam ibn Hisham or by Umar ibn al-Khattab, and said the Prophet was in a house by Safa. Umar took his sword and went to that house and knocked at the door (p. 345). The account runs on to the moment he accepts Islam on the next page, which was not read for this audit. The Prophet's ﷺ dream of a palace in Paradise that he was told was Umar's is in Sahih al-Bukhari 3680.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Umar went to the door with a sword and was met by a page of the Qur'an. When did something you read change the errand you were on?

title: Taif
subtitle: Driven to a vineyard — and he hoped for their descendants
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1 pp. 419-420 (the journey to Ta'if; the vineyard; the supplication), read on shamela.ws, book 23833
Sahih al-Bukhari 3231 — the day of Aqabah and the angel of the mountains

chapters.heading: The Saddest Day of the Seerah
chapters.body: After Abu Talib died, Quraysh harmed the Prophet ﷺ more than they had before, and he went out to Ta'if to seek the support of Thaqif (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 p. 419). Thaqif stirred up their fools and slaves against him, cursing and shouting at him, and drove him into a vineyard belonging to Utba and Shayba, sons of Rabi'a (p. 420). There, in Ibn Ishaq's account, he prayed: 'O Allah, to You I complain of my weakness, my lack of resources and my humiliation before the people... If You are not displeased with me, then I do not care' (p. 420). In another report Aisha asks whether he had faced a day harder than Uhud, and he answers that the worst was the day of Aqabah; the angel of the mountains is offered to him at Qarn al-Tha'alib, and he declines, hoping that Allah will bring from their descendants people who worship Allah alone (Bukhari 3231; the hadith itself does not name Ta'if or mention stones). Other reports, not checked here: that he was stoned and bled, that the mountain-angel scene took place on this journey, and that a delegation from Ta'if later accepted Islam.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: The man they stoned prayed for their grandchildren. Is there someone who hurt you whose children you could still bless?

title: The Pledges of Aqabah
subtitle: Seventy-five hands in the dark — Madinah accepts the message
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1 pp. 429, 433, 434, 441 and 443 (the six, the twelve, Mus'ab, the second pledge, the twelve leaders), read on shamela.ws, book 23833
Sahih al-Bukhari 18 — the pledge of Aqabah: no shirk, theft, adultery, killing children, slander or disobedience in good (narrated by Ubadah ibn al-Samit)

chapters.heading: Twelve, Then Seventy-Five
chapters.body: At the pilgrimage season the Prophet ﷺ met six men of the Khazraj at Aqabah, among them As'ad ibn Zurara and Rafi' ibn Malik. Ibn Ishaq says they told one another that this was the prophet the Jews had threatened them with, and that they had left a people among whom there was enmity and evil, hoping Allah would unite them through him (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 p. 429). The next year twelve men met him at Aqabah. Ubada ibn al-Samit says: 'we were twelve men', and the pledge was the like of the women's pledge, before fighting was prescribed: not to associate anything with Allah, not to steal, not to commit adultery, not to kill their children (p. 433; also Sahih al-Bukhari 18, in the wording: no shirk, theft, adultery, killing children, slander or disobedience in good). The Prophet ﷺ sent Mus'ab ibn Umayr with them, ordering him to teach them the Qur'an and Islam and to give them understanding in the religion; Asim ibn Umar reports that he used to lead them in prayer (p. 434). The next year the pilgrims of Yathrib came again; a narrator says: 'we were seventy-three men, and with us two women', and that they slipped out secretly after a third of the night and gathered in the ravine at Aqabah, where al-Abbas, still on his people's religion, spoke first and asked them to protect his nephew only if they could keep their promise (p. 441). The Prophet ﷺ then had twelve leaders chosen, nine from the Khazraj and three from the Aws (p. 443). The Ansar of Madinah were preparing a city before the Prophet ﷺ had ever seen it.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: The Ansar believed in a man they had met twice. What makes someone trustworthy enough to follow?

title: The Hijrah
subtitle: The cave, the companion, and the man who rode for a bounty
sources: Qur'an 9:40 — 'the second of two, when they were in the cave' (revealed for this night)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3905 — the Hijrah with Abu Bakr, including three nights in the cave
Sahih al-Bukhari 3653 — Abu Bakr in the cave: 'what do you think of two whose third is Allah'
Sahih al-Bukhari 3906 — Suraqa, the sinking horse and the written pledge
Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa, al-Abyari and al-Shalabi), vol. 1 pp. 482, 485, 489-490 and 492, read on shamela.ws, book 23833

chapters.heading: The Second of Two
chapters.body: The Prophet ﷺ left Makkah with Abu Bakr and entered a cave in Mount Thawr, below the city (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 p. 485). Ibn Ishaq, as Ibn Hisham gives it, has Abu Jahl propose that Quraysh take one strong, well-born young man from every clan to strike together, so that Banu Abd Manaf could not fight all of Quraysh and would settle for the blood-price (vol. 1 p. 482). In the cave Abu Bakr's son listened by day to what people said of them, and Asma bint Abi Bakr brought food at nightfall (p. 485). Bukhari 3905 has them stay in the cave three nights. In Bukhari 3653 Abu Bakr says that if one of the pursuers looked down at his own feet he would see them, and the Prophet ﷺ answers: what do you think of two whose third is Allah? The Qur'an keeps his words: 'Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us', and says Allah supported him with soldiers you did not see (9:40). Later tradition adds a spider's web and a dove's nest at the entrance; these are not in the Qur'an, in Bukhari 3905 or in the pages read, and no chain was verified for this audit. Ibn Hisham reports Quraysh offering a hundred camels to whoever brought him back (p. 489). In Suraqa ibn Malik's own account there, his horse stumbled and threw him three times, and the third time its forelegs sank into the ground; he asked for a written pledge, and the Prophet ﷺ told Abu Bakr to write it, on a bone, a scrap or a potsherd (pp. 489-490). Suraqa put it in his quiver, went back and kept silent about what he had seen. Bukhari 3906 also has the horse's forelegs sink and the written pledge. The two reached Quba, among Banu Amr ibn Awf, on a Monday in Rabi' al-Awwal; Ibn Hisham gives the twelfth night, and a footnote notes that some say the eighth (p. 492).
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Allah's help in the cave came without any visible guard. What unseen help have you only noticed looking back?

title: The Arrival in Madinah
subtitle: The city rejoiced: the Messenger has arrived
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1 pp. 494-496 (Quba, the camel, Abu Ayyub), read on shamela.ws, book 23833
Sahih al-Bukhari 3925 — the joy of Madinah at his arrival (al-Bara' ibn Azib)
Sahih al-Bukhari 2048 — Sa'd ibn al-Rabi' and Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf: half the wealth, 'show me the market'
Qur'an 9:108 — 'a mosque founded on righteousness from the first day'

chapters.heading: A City That Ran to Meet Him
chapters.body: At Quba the Prophet ﷺ stayed, by Ibn Hisham's account, from Monday to Thursday (Banu Amr ibn Awf claimed he stayed longer) and founded his mosque there, which a footnote calls the first mosque built in Islam (vol. 1 p. 494); the Qur'an honors a mosque 'founded on righteousness from the first day' (9:108). Then he rode toward Madinah. Clan after clan stopped his camel and invited him to stay with them, speaking of their numbers, strength and protection, and each time he answered: 'Let her go her way, for she is commanded' (pp. 494-495). The camel knelt at the gate of the mosque-site in the house of Banu Malik ibn al-Najjar; he did not dismount, it rose, walked a little, then turned back and knelt in the same place, and he got down; Abu Ayyub al-Ansari carried his saddle into his house (pp. 495-496). Al-Bara' ibn Azib said he had never seen the people of Madinah rejoice as they did: even the slave girls were saying that the Messenger of Allah had arrived (Bukhari 3925). The Ansar and Muhajirun were paired as brothers. In one hadith the Ansari Sa'd ibn al-Rabi' offered Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf half of his wealth; Abd al-Rahman declined and asked only where the market was, and the Prophet ﷺ later told him to hold a wedding feast, even with one sheep (Bukhari 2048). The first economy of Madinah, then, began with an offer of half and an answer of 'show me the market'.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Sa'd offered half of everything and Abd al-Rahman asked only for the market. What would you genuinely share, and what would you refuse and still be grateful for?

title: The Charter of Madinah
subtitle: One document, one ummah — many faiths under one covenant
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the text of the Charter (sahifa)

chapters.heading: Writing a Nation
chapters.body: Within the first year, the Prophet ﷺ did something no conqueror does: he sat with the Jewish clans of Madinah and wrote a charter — the Sahifa — making one ummah of the believers and the Jews, each with their religion and their alliances, one hand against any aggressor, disputes referred to Allah and His Messenger. Abdullah ibn Salam, a Jewish scholar of Madinah, embraced Islam in these early days (his own account is in the hadith literature; the number and wording were not re-checked here). For a time, Madinah lived the experiment: one city, many religions, one covenant. The hypocrites — those who said with their mouths what their hearts denied (63:1) — tested it from within, and some clan leaders tested it from without, until the covenant's clauses were broken one by one and its sanctions came due one by one. But the document itself stands in history: a remarkable early written covenant for a plural city, in the reports that preserve it.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: The Charter made one nation of different faiths. What community are you part of that needs one covenant more than it needs one religion?

title: The Qibla Changes
subtitle: Sixteen months toward Jerusalem — then one command turned a congregation around
sources: Qur'an 2:142-150 — the whole passage, 'We see the turning of your face'
Sahih al-Bukhari 399 — the change of the qiblah

chapters.heading: Turning the Whole Community
chapters.body: For sixteen or seventeen months in Madinah (Bukhari 399), the Muslims prayed toward Jerusalem — the qiblah of Ibrahim and Musa. Some people were not content with it. And the Prophet ﷺ, who used to face the heavens waiting for the command, received it mid-prayer: a prayer (placing it in a zuhr prayer at the mosque of Banu Salama is a later tradition we have not verified), during which the verse descended — 'So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram' (2:144) — and the worshippers turned toward Makkah mid-prayer (Bukhari 399). Allah framed the change itself as revelation about revelation: 'We see the turning of your face to heaven, so We will surely turn you to a qiblah with which you will be pleased' (2:144) — and then taught the deeper lesson: it is not righteousness to face east or west (2:177). And the fools said, 'What has turned them from their qiblah?' — to which the answer came: 'Say: to Allah belong the east and the west; He guides whom He wills to a straight path' (2:142).

familyQuestion: The whole congregation turned mid-prayer without arguing. When has your community changed direction without splitting?

title: Badr: The Two Armies Meet
subtitle: A little over three hundred against some nine hundred to a thousand
sources: Qur'an 3:123-127 — 'Allah already gave you victory at Badr'
Qur'an 8:41 — 'what We bestowed upon you on the day of the criterion'
Sahih al-Bukhari 3959 — the companions at Badr numbered over three hundred and ten (al-Bara')
Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1 pp. 617, 626 and 627, read on shamela.ws, book 23833

chapters.heading: The Criterion
chapters.body: The Qur'an later named the day: 'the day of the criterion — furqan — the day the two hosts met' (8:41). The Muslims were a little over three hundred and ten (Bukhari 3959, from al-Bara'), against Quraysh, whom a scout reported as between nine hundred and a thousand (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 p. 617). On the morning of the battle the Prophet ﷺ was straightening the ranks with an arrow in his hand; he prodded Sawad ibn Ghaziyya in the belly to bring him into line, and Sawad asked to take his retaliation, which the Prophet ﷺ allowed (p. 626). Then, in the shelter built for him, he pleaded with his Lord for the victory promised: 'O Allah, if this band perishes today You will not be worshipped'; Abu Bakr told him that was enough pleading, for Allah would fulfil what He promised (p. 627). The Qur'an records the other side of that morning: 'Indeed, Allah had already given you victory at Badr while you were few in number... that Allah might accomplish a matter already destined' (3:123, 126). Three thousand angels, it says — 'and Allah made it but glad tidings so that your hearts would be assured, and victory is only from Allah' (3:126).
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: Allah sent angels but said victory is only from Him. When you win, who do you thank first?

title: Badr: The Prisoners
subtitle: The prisoners of Badr: 'treat them well'
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 1 p. 645 (the prisoners distributed; 'treat them well'; Abu Aziz and the bread), read on shamela.ws, book 23833
Qur'an 8:67-71 — 'it is not for a prophet to have captives until he inflicts slaughter'

chapters.heading: Mercy After Victory
chapters.body: The battle was over and the prisoners were taken. Ibn Ishaq reports that the Prophet ﷺ distributed the prisoners among his companions and said: 'Treat the prisoners well' (Ibn Hisham, vol. 1 p. 645). Abu Aziz ibn Umayr, one of them, later said that the men who held him gave him the bread at their meals while they ate dates themselves (p. 645). A report that the Prophet ﷺ set the ransom of some literate prisoners at teaching Muslim children to read is told elsewhere; it is not on the pages read here and its source was not checked. The revelation that came about the day named the tension honestly: 'It is not for a prophet to have captives until he inflicts slaughter in the land' (8:67). But the surah goes on to the law that outlasted the battle: 'So consume what you have taken of spoils, lawful and good, and fear Allah' (8:69) — and to the prisoners themselves: 'if Allah knows any good in your hearts, He will give you better than what was taken from you' (8:70).
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: The Prophet ﷺ told his companions to treat their prisoners well, and they gave them the bread. When did you last do the generous thing for someone who had lost to you?

title: Uhud: The Day the Line Broke
subtitle: Archers leave the pass — and the Prophet ﷺ bleeds on the mountain
sources: Qur'an 3:152-155 — the day 'some of you desired the world'
Qur'an 3:144 — 'Muhammad is not but a messenger; messengers have passed on before him'
Sahih al-Bukhari 4043-4044 — the archers who left their post at Uhud

chapters.heading: The Turning
chapters.body: The archers held the pass behind the Muslims as ordered — until the spoils of the routed enemy appeared, and most of them descended, against orders, for their share. Khalid ibn al-Walid, still an enemy commander that day, saw the pass empty and wheeled his cavalry through it. The Muslim line broke from behind; Hamza, the master of martyrs, fell; and the Prophet ﷺ — wounded in the face, a tooth broken, rumor running the field that he had been killed — stood on the slope with the remnant around him. The verse descended that anchors the whole religion: 'Muhammad is not but a messenger; messengers have passed on before him. So if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?' (3:144). The Muslims rallied to the slope; the Quraysh withdrew. And the revelation's verdict on the day named the lesson every generation inherits: 'Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you when you were killing them by His permission until you lost courage and fell into dispute and disobeyed' (3:152) — victory had come by obedience; its near-loss came by desire. The spoils of Uhud were a Qur'an.

familyQuestion: The archers left their post for spoils and nearly lost everything. What 'post' are you tempted to leave right now?

title: Uhud: Hamza and the Women
subtitle: The master of martyrs, the mutilated dead, and Hind's answer
sources: Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 2 pp. 91, 95-96 (Hind; the Prophet and Hamza; the prohibition of mutilation), read on shamela.ws, book 23833
Sahih al-Bukhari 4072 — Wahshi's account of killing Hamza
Sahih al-Bukhari 3825 — Hind bint Utba after she embraced Islam
Qur'an 16:126-128 — 'if you punish, punish with the like of that with which you were afflicted'

chapters.heading: The Lion and the Lesson
chapters.body: Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet's ﷺ uncle, was killed at Uhud by a thrown spear: Wahshi, a slave of Jubayr ibn Mut'im who had been promised his freedom for it, tells how he drove the spear in (Bukhari 4072). Ibn Ishaq says the Prophet ﷺ went looking for him and found him in the valley with his belly cut open, his liver taken out, his nose and ears cut off (Ibn Hisham, vol. 2 p. 95). Ibn Hisham also names Hind bint Utba as the one who made anklets and necklaces from the ears and noses of the dead and who cut into Hamza's liver (p. 91). Ibn Ishaq has the Prophet ﷺ say, seeing him, that were it not for Safiyya's grief and for the precedent it would set, he would leave him for the beasts and the birds (p. 95); and then swear that if Allah gave him victory over Quraysh he would mutilate thirty of their men (pp. 95-96). The Muslims said the same. Then came the revelation: 'And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were punished; but if you are patient, it is better for the patient' (16:126). Ibn Hisham states that the Prophet ﷺ forbade mutilation (p. 96). Hind bint Utba later came to him and said that before she embraced Islam there was no household on earth she wished to see disgraced more than his, and now none she wished to see honored more (Bukhari 3825).
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: The Prophet ﷺ was told that patience is better than the revenge he had sworn. What revenge habit could your family end with you?

title: The Trench
subtitle: Ten thousand at the walls — and a biting wind from the unseen
sources: Qur'an 33:9-27 — 'when they came at you from above and below'
Qur'an 33:10-11 — 'there the believers were tested and shaken with a severe shaking'
Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the digging of the trench

chapters.heading: The Severe Shaking
chapters.body: Madinah had a side the armies could not cross — the lava fields and the palm groves — and the Prophet ﷺ, taking the advice of Salman the Persian, ordered a trench dug along the open quarter. The believers dug through the cold nights, and the hypocrites stood at the edge bargaining: a trench against the horsemen of Quraysh? — 'that is what the Persians do' (Ibn Ishaq). Then the alliance arrived: ten thousand — Quraysh from the south, Ghatafan from the east, with chiefs of the exiled Jewish clan of Banu Nadir having helped to rally them (a seerah report). The Qur'an preserved the city at its breaking point: 'When they came at you from above you and from below you, and when eyes swerved and hearts reached the throats, and you assumed about Allah various assumptions. There the believers were tested and shaken with a severe shaking' (33:10-11). And then, at the height of the siege — with the trench holding, with Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud sowing distrust between the allies as a new Muslim working from inside — the wind came: a bitter gale that blew for days, freezing the besiegers in their camps and tearing their tents, until the alliance dissolved and marched away without a battle being fought (33:9). Madinah had not won the Trench. Allah had.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: The trench held because Salman, a Persian outsider, was listened to. Whose 'outsider' idea are you ignoring right now?

title: Hudaybiyyah
subtitle: The treaty that looked like defeat — and the sura named a clear conquest
sources: Qur'an 48:1-3 — 'Indeed, We have given you a clear conquest'
Sahih al-Bukhari 2731-2732 — the terms of the treaty of Hudaybiyyah and Umar's objection
Sahih al-Bukhari 4154 — about fourteen hundred men (Jabir)
Sahih al-Bukhari 4177 — a sura revealed on the journey (Al-Fath)
Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 2 pp. 316-318 (the truce, the ten years, Umar's question and the reply), read on shamela.ws, book 23833

chapters.heading: The Clear Conquest
chapters.body: The Prophet ﷺ set out for Makkah to perform umrah in peace with about fourteen hundred men (Bukhari 4154, from Jabir) — and Quraysh barred them from the House at Hudaybiyyah (Bukhari 2731). The treaty that followed looked like surrender. Quraysh insisted that he go back that year (Ibn Hisham, vol. 2 p. 316). In the text Ibn Hisham gives, the two sides agreed to put war away from the people for ten years, in which people would be safe; and a man of Quraysh who came to Muhammad without his guardian's permission would be returned, while one who went to Quraysh would not (p. 317). Bukhari 2731 has the same clause that Suhayl demanded, even if the man had embraced Islam. Umar ibn al-Khattab could not bear it. In Bukhari 2731 he asks whether their cause is not the right one and the enemy's wrong. In Ibn Hisham he asks: why should we accept humiliation in our religion? And the Prophet ﷺ answers: 'I am the servant of Allah and His Messenger; I will not disobey His command, and He will not let me be lost' (p. 317). Bukhari 4177 records that on a night journey a sura was revealed to him and he recited its opening: the sura of Al-Fath, which Bukhari files under the Hudaybiyyah expedition. The Qur'an named what no eye could see: 'Indeed, We have given you a clear conquest' (48:1). Two years later the Muslims entered Makkah.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: The treaty everyone hated opened the doors of Arabia. Have you ever had a 'defeat' that was actually a door?

title: The Letters to the Rulers
subtitle: The letter that reached the Emperor of Rome
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the letters to the rulers
Sahih al-Bukhari 2941 — the letter to Heraclius

chapters.heading: From the Prophet of Mercy
chapters.body: After Hudaybiyyah, the Prophet ﷺ began the last stage of the mission — writing to the rulers of the world. The letter to Heraclius, Emperor of Rome, survives in the Sahih: 'In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful. From Muhammad, the servant of Allah and His Messenger, to Heraclius the Great of Rome. Peace be upon those who follow guidance... I call you to Islam: become Muslim and you will be safe, and Allah will double your reward; but if you turn away, you bear the sins of the peasants' (Bukhari 2941). Heraclius did not convert — but the hadith of Abu Sufyan (Sahih al-Bukhari; number not re-checked here) records that he questioned Abu Sufyan about the Prophet ﷺ. Other kings answered differently: the Negus of Abyssinia, who had sheltered the emigrants, embraced Islam before he died; the governor of Egypt, al-Muqawqis, sent gifts and courtesy but not faith; the ruler of Persia tore the letter. Khaybar, a Jewish stronghold north of Madinah, was taken in the same year (a seerah report; the terms and aftermath are not told here because they were not checked).
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: The Prophet ﷺ wrote 'become Muslim and you will be safe' to the most powerful men alive. What does that tell you about the mission — fear, or invitation?

title: The Conquest of Makkah
subtitle: Eight years after being driven out — he enters with his head bowed
sources: Qur'an 110 — 'When the victory of Allah has come and the conquest'
Sahih al-Bukhari 4280 — Abu Sufyan sees the Muslim forces enter Makkah; the Prophet's ﷺ flag at al-Hajun
Seerah: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa et al.), vol. 2 pp. 400, 406, 409, 412 and 413 (the march, the entry, the orders, the address, the pictures), read on shamela.ws, book 23833

chapters.heading: The Day of Mercy
chapters.body: In Ramadan of the eighth year the Prophet ﷺ camped at Marr al-Zahran with ten thousand Muslims (Ibn Hisham, vol. 2 p. 400). Bukhari 4280 has Abu Sufyan watching the Muslim forces pass. He ordered his commanders to fight only those who fought them, and named a few individuals who were to be killed (p. 409). The army went in by separate roads; when Sa'd ibn Ubada said that today was a day of slaughter, Umar warned the Prophet ﷺ, who stood to answer (p. 406). Ibn Hisham gives the Prophet's ﷺ address to Quraysh: he asked what they thought he would do with them, they answered with kindness, and he said: 'Go, for you are the freed ones' (p. 412). He ordered the pictures in the House effaced (p. 413). Surah An-Nasr speaks of that victory: 'When the victory of Allah has come and the conquest, and you see the people entering into the religion of Allah in multitudes, then exalt your Lord and ask His forgiveness. Indeed, He is ever accepting of repentance' (110:1-3). Other details told of the day, not checked here: his head lowered on his mount, reciting Al-Fath; the idols of the Kaaba cast down by his hand; the Qurayshi breach of the truce that began the campaign.
chapters.label: Seerah report

familyQuestion: He entered the city that tried to kill him and said 'you are free.' Who in your life deserves amnesty you have the power to give?

title: Hunayn and Taif
subtitle: Victory at Hunayn, and a city that later came to Islam
sources: Qur'an 9:25-27 — 'Allah has already given you victory in many regions'
Reported in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim — the Prophet's ﷺ words to the Ansar after Hunayn (hadith numbers not re-checked in this build)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3231 — 'I hope that Allah will bring from their descendants people who will worship Allah alone'

chapters.heading: The Spoils and the Sweetness
chapters.body: After Makkah came Hunayn, against the Hawazin with their families and herds behind them — a new army with new wealth, and the first shock of the battle was a near-rout until the Prophet ﷺ stood firm on his mule calling the fleeing ranks back (9:25-27). The spoils of Hunayn were the richest of the Prophet's ﷺ life, and he distributed them to the hearts he was still winning — the new Makkan elite — until the Ansar, who had carried the faith in its hungriest years, murmured: he has given Quraysh and left us. He called them and said the words that settled their hearts and built their legend: are you not pleased that the people go home with sheep and camels, and you go home with the Messenger of Allah? — and they wept and said: yes, we are pleased with the Messenger of Allah (reported in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). Then the Prophet ﷺ marched to Taif, whose people had once turned him away; the siege was lifted without the city falling, and the people of Taif later sent a delegation and accepted Islam (seerah reports; details not checked here). The hope he voiced long before — that Allah would bring from their descendants people who would worship Allah alone — is recorded in Bukhari 3231.
chapters.label: Seerah report (source not checked)

familyQuestion: The Ansar were offered 'the Messenger of Allah' instead of wealth — and wept with joy. What would you take in place of money?

title: Tabuk
subtitle: The hardest march — and the hypocrites unmasked
sources: Qur'an 9:38-59 — the whole passage of the expedition
Qur'an 9:117-118 — 'then He turned to him in forgiveness'

chapters.heading: The Expedition of Hardship
chapters.body: In the heat of the ripening fruit season, news came that the Byzantines were massing at the northern border — and the Prophet ﷺ called the Muslims to the hardest expedition of his life: Tabuk, in the scorching end of summer, with the orchards heavy and the harvest calling. The hypocrites stayed behind with excuses, and the Qur'an unmasked them permanently in Surah At-Tawbah: 'If you do not go forth, He will punish you with a painful punishment and replace you with another people' (9:39). Three believers who stayed behind without excuse — Ka'b ibn Malik and his two companions — were boycotted by the entire city, by order of the Prophet ﷺ, for fifty days, until the revelation came down forgiving them: 'and to the three who were left behind, until the earth closed upon them... then He turned to them in forgiveness' (9:118). Tabuk was the last expedition of the Prophet's ﷺ life, and its lesson stands at the summit of the seerah: the community is measured not by the battles it wins but by the accountability it survives — even its greatest men were disciplined publicly, and even their repentance was written into the Qur'an for all time.
chapters.label: Hadith report (reference not checked)

familyQuestion: Ka'b ibn Malik's punishment became a verse of forgiveness. What mistake of yours could become your testimony?

title: The Farewell Sermon
subtitle: One speech, one standing — the charter of every Muslim generation
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 67 — the Prophet's ﷺ sermon on the sanctity of lives, wealth and honor
Sahih Muslim 1218 — Jabir's account of the Prophet's ﷺ Hajj and the Farewell address

chapters.heading: Listen Well, for I May Not Meet You Again Here
chapters.body: In the tenth year, the Prophet ﷺ performed his only full pilgrimage, and at Arafat, standing on his camel, he delivered the sermon that is the constitution of the ummah. The tradition preserves it: every Muslim's blood, property, and honor are inviolable, like this day, in this month, in this city; no usury from this day; no blood feud from this day; women have rights over you as you have rights over them; your brother's blood and property are sacred (Bukhari 67, Muslim 1218). Then he asked: have I conveyed? — and the valley answered: yes. And he raised his finger to the sky and said: O Allah, bear witness; O Allah, bear witness. And he told them, while he still stood before them healthy: those who are present must convey it to those who are absent — and he would be with them for only a few months more. The sermon of Arafat is remembered because it gathers, in one address, the dignity of life, wealth and honor.

familyQuestion: The Prophet ﷺ said your brother's blood and property are sacred. Whose rights are you trampling right now without noticing?

title: The Passing of the Prophet ﷺ
subtitle: The house of Aisha, the sword of Umar, and the steadiness of Abu Bakr
sources: Qur'an 3:144 — 'if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?'

chapters.heading: Monday
chapters.body: The fever came in Safar of the eleventh year, after the farewell pilgrimage. For days the Prophet ﷺ grew weaker in the house of Aisha, sometimes joining the prayers seated, then directing Abu Bakr to lead the community in his place (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim; numbers not re-checked here) — a command the early Muslims later recalled when Abu Bakr was chosen as leader. On Monday, with his head in Aisha's lap, he raised his eyes and said: rather, the Highest Companion (Aisha's account, reported in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim; numbers not re-checked here) — and the greatest life in history ended with a choice: the prayer, or the Companion above. Umar stood and refused to believe it: he has not died; he has gone to his Lord as Musa went (Sahih al-Bukhari; number not re-checked here). Abu Bakr came from his house at al-Sunh, uncovered the Prophet's ﷺ face, kissed his forehead, and said: may my father and mother be sacrificed for you; by Allah, Allah will never cause you to die twice — then he recited the verse that had descended at Uhud for exactly this hour: 'Muhammad is not but a messenger; messengers have passed on before him' (3:144). The mosque of Madinah filled with weeping; the question of leadership was settled at the porch of Banu Sa'ida; and the man who had entered every city as a stranger left the world in the room of the wife he loved most, among his family, on his own bed, at peace. The tradition records that the day was Monday — the day of his birth.
chapters.label: Hadith report (reference not checked)

familyQuestion: Umar denied it; Abu Bakr recited Qur'an. When grief hits your family, which one will you be?

title: What He Left
subtitle: No palace, no hoard, no empire in his name — and an ummah that outlives empires
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 2739 — the Prophet ﷺ left no money, only his mule, his weapons and a charitable land endowment
Sahih al-Bukhari 3092 — 'what we leave is charity'

chapters.heading: The Inventory of a Prophet
chapters.body: He died owning a mended cloak, a couch of palm-fiber that left marks on his side, a handful of barley, and a debt — his shield was still in pawn to a Jew of Madinah for the food of his household (the estate he left: Sahih al-Bukhari 2739; the cloak, the couch and the pawned shield are reported in Sahih al-Bukhari). A report preserves his last counsel as: the prayer, and those in your charge (collection and number not checked here). He left no son to inherit his authority and no fortune to divide: 'We, the company of prophets, leave no inheritance; what we leave is charity' (Sahih al-Bukhari 3092). Within thirty years of his death, his companions ruled from Egypt and Syria to Persia; within a century, the languages of three continents recited his book; within fourteen centuries, his followers number well over a billion. He left no statue of himself — the tradition forbids his image — and so the world built no monument to Muhammad except the practice of his message. In words reported from him: 'I have only been sent to perfect noble character' (reported by Ahmad; the number was not verified).
chapters.label: Hadith report (reference not checked)

familyQuestion: He left no inheritance but character. What will your children inherit from you that money can't buy?

title: Reflections: The Man Who Walked Beside Us
subtitle: Thirty chapters, one walk — what it means to follow him ﷺ
sources: Musnad Ahmad — 'I have only been sent to perfect noble character' (number not verified)
Sahih Muslim 45 — none of you truly believes until he wishes for his brother what he wishes for himself
Qur'an 33:21 — 'There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example'

chapters.heading: The Example
chapters.body: The Qur'an does not say the Prophet ﷺ was perfect so you could worship him. It says: 'There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example — uswa hasana — for those who hope in Allah and the Last Day and remember Allah often' (33:21). An example is for following. He was an orphan, so the orphan is honored. He was a merchant, so the scale is straight. He was driven from his city, so the stranger is sheltered. He was stoned, so the wounded are comforted. He conquered, so the conquered are forgiven. He ruled, so rulers are accountable. He died poor, so the poor are honored. Thirty chapters walked past like thirty footsteps — and the invitation of every one of them is the same: walk here. Not in his century, but in his character. One way to answer the question — what did he leave us? — is: nothing you can hold, and everything you can become.
chapters.label: Reflection

familyQuestion: Thirty chapters end here. Which single habit of his ﷺ — honesty, gentleness, patience, courage, mercy — will your family practice together this week?

title: Iqra — The First Word
subtitle: The first word of the final message was not 'believe' or 'obey' — it was 'read'
sources: Qur'an 96:1-5

chapters.heading: A Cave, a Covering, a Voice
chapters.body: Muhammad ﷺ had taken to the cave of Hira, seeking quiet from a city that troubled him. In Ramadan, at forty, the angel came to him, pressed him, and said one word: 'Iqra — Read' (96:1). The man who would be called unlettered received a command built on the written word. Whatever else the world would say about this religion, its first word was an act of the mind.

chapters.heading: The Name of Your Lord
chapters.body: The reply to 'I cannot read' was not a scolding. It was the material itself: 'Read in the name of your Lord who created — created man from a clinging substance. Read, and your Lord is the most Generous, who taught by the pen — taught man that which he knew not' (96:1-5). Name first, then knowledge. Every act of learning in this deen begins with whose name is on it.

chapters.heading: What the First Word Decided
chapters.body: Notice what the first revelation did not say. Not 'rule', not 'conquer', not 'gather followers'. Read, in the name of your Lord. The command that launched a civilization made literacy an act of worship and inquiry a form of devotion. The Prophet ﷺ came home trembling, and Khadijah held him and said what the moment required: 'Allah will never disgrace you — you keep kinship, you carry the weak.' The first word chose knowledge; the first home chose comfort. The message has lived in both ever since.

familyQuestion: What are we 'reading' in our home this month — and in whose name do we begin?
